message.abstract:
<jats:title>Fast phase change with no preconditions</jats:title>
          <jats:p>
            Random access memory (RAM) devices that rely on phase changes are primarily limited by the speed of crystallization. Rao
            <jats:italic>et al.</jats:italic>
            combined theory with a simple set of selection criteria to isolate a scandium-doped antimony telluride (SST) with a subnanosecond crystallization speed (see the Perspective by Akola and Jones). They synthesized SST and constructed a RAM device with a 700-picosecond writing speed. This is an order of magnitude faster than previous phase-change memory devices and competitive with consumer dynamic access, static random access, and flash memory.
          </jats:p>
          <jats:p>
            <jats:italic>Science</jats:italic>
            , this issue p.
            <jats:related-article xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="doi" issue="6369" page="1423" related-article-type="in-this-issue" vol="358" xlink:href="10.1126/science.aao3212">1423</jats:related-article>
            ; see also p.
            <jats:related-article xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="doi" issue="6369" page="1386" related-article-type="in-this-issue" vol="358" xlink:href="10.1126/science.aaq0476">1386</jats:related-article>
          </jats:p>
title: Reducing the stochasticity of crystal nucleation to enable subnanosecond memory writing
